items.title: 66600_Teddy Wilson oral history interview
items.q: Fred Robins, who used to be the greatest jazz jockey in America, he's working overseas with that stuff, and I hear him all the time, he's interviewing movie stars... And here he is asking Paul McCartney

ctx.x: But those things, see, they flare up like a big rocket and they flare right down -- for six weeks or so, just like Tiny Tim, you know, and it's a temporary thing. It's hard to repeat; it's hard for Tiny Tim to establish a career doing that, that was a one time thing -- 'Tiptoe Through the Tulips'. It's not a solid thing like jazz is, real jazz or classical music, that carries you on, it never hits a giant sale like 'Tiptoe Through the Tulips.' No jazz record would ever sell like that, I guess, but it will go on…
hear Fred Robins with the American Armed Forces doing a stupid thing called The Sign of Hollywood. Today he was interviewing Paul McCartney -- how does it feel when you hear a Beatles record?

Fred Robins, who used to be the greatest jazz jockey in America, he's working overseas with that stuff, and I hear him all the time, he's interviewing movie stars, the most nobody people, and asking them the most stupid questions like you would see in Screen Love magazine or something. Fred Robins, the best disc jockey that this country ever had, to me, when he was down in New York. I mean, the boys wrote Robin's Nest and dedicated it to him, Jacquet and Charlie Thompson.
